Stage 3 · Grammar

What you must do, and what you simply don’t have to

Four forms. Two of them look similar and mean the opposite.

Read these four sentences about a school.
  • Teachers must have a master’s degree.
  • Students have to pass an entrance exam.
  • A teacher doesn’t have to follow a national plan.
  • Private schools can’t charge fees.
Look at sentences 3 and 4. What is the difference?
The four meanings
MeaningFormExampleQuestion
It is necessary

The pasthad to for all of them: I had to take an exam. · I didn’t have to take an exam.  There is no past of must.
the obligation word the plain verb

FORM. must and mustn’t are modals: no -s, no to, no do in the question. have to is a normal verb: has to, had to, do you have to…?

USE. must / have to = it is necessary · don’t have to = it is not necessary · mustn’t / can’t = it is forbidden · can = it is allowed.

The pair that matters: You mustn’t pay (it is forbidden) is not You don’t have to pay (it is free).

Advice — should and why don’t you — comes in Lesson 27, and it uses the same plain verb after it.

FORM. must is a modal, like can in the last lesson: it never adds -s, never takes to after it, and makes its question by changing the word order. have to is an ordinary verb, so it changes like one: I have to, she has to, we had to, do you have to…?, she doesn’t have to.

USE — necessary. must usually carries a rule you give yourself (I must call my mother) or a written rule (Passengers must show a ticket). have to carries a rule that comes from outside you (I have to be at work at eight). In everyday speech have to is far more common; you will rarely be wrong with it.

USE — the two negatives. This is the whole lesson. don’t have to = there is no obligation, you are free: You don’t have to wear a uniform — wear what you like. mustn’t = there is an obligation not to: You mustn’t wear a uniform — it is not allowed. The two look alike and mean the opposite.

Three mistakes to watch: “I must to go” (no to after a modal) · “He have to work” (it is has to) · “I musted study” (there is no past of must — use had to).

In Lesson 27 the same plain verb comes back after should and ought to for advice.

Full grammar reference — must, have to, don’t have to, can’t

Form

NecessaryYou must wear a uniform. · You have to pass an exam.
Third personShe has to work on Saturdays.
Not necessaryYou don’t have to come. · He doesn’t have to pay.
ForbiddenYou mustn’t smoke here. · You can’t park here. · You’re not allowed to use a phone.
QuestionDo I have to book? · Short answer: Yes, you do. / No, you don’t.

When and why we use it

  • Have to usually points to a rule that comes from outside — the school, the law, the job.
  • Must often points to the speaker’s own feeling that something is necessary: I must call my mother.
  • Must has no past. Use had to: I had to leave early.
  • Questions and negatives of have to are made with do / does / did.

Signal words

rules · it’s necessary · it’s not necessary · it’s forbidden · you’re allowed to

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • You must to wear a uniform. → You must wear a uniform.No to after must.
  • You haven’t to come. → You don’t have to come.Have to is negated with don’t.
  • She have to work. → She has to work.Third person.
  • I musted go. → I had to go.Must has no past form.

Don’t confuse it with

The most important pair in this unit. You don’t have to come = it is your choice. You mustn’t come = it is forbidden. They are opposites, not variations.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

One country took most of the rules away. Then it kept one.

Before you read: one country has almost no school exams before the age of eighteen.

What do you think happened to its results? Decide first, then read and find out.

There is no right answer yet. This is your prediction.

The country that took the rules away

In most school systems the rules are easy to see. You have to wear a uniform. You must be in your seat when the bell rings. You have to pass an entrance exam to get into a good school, and you have to sit tests every year to prove that you deserve your grade.

Finland decided to try something else. Finnish children do not start school until they are seven. They don’t have to take a single national exam until they are about eighteen. Nearly every child goes to a state school, and the few private schools that exist are not allowed to charge fees, so parents cannot buy a better education. Homework is light. The school day is short.

But one rule in Finland is very strict. To stand in front of a class, a teacher must have a master’s degree, and the courses that train them are harder to get into than law or medicine. A Finnish teacher doesn’t have to follow a national plan hour by hour — they can choose how to teach their own subject — because the system trusts a qualification it made difficult to get.

Its success surprised everybody. For twenty years Finland has been near the top of the international tests in reading, maths and science, with less testing than almost anyone else.

Nobody says the country is perfect, and its results have fallen a little since 2006. Copying it is not simple either: a system that trusts its teachers has to build that trust first, and that takes a generation. But the lesson is not that rules are bad. It is that a system has to decide where the rules belong — in the classroom, or in the choice of the person standing in it.

Sources. Finnish National Agency for Education, Education system · OECD PISA 2000–2022 country notes for Finland · Basic Education Act (Finland), on fees in private schools. Text written for this course.
